parts:
I’m really sorry you’re dealing with this. What you’re describing is not normal communication or progress for a case like this, especially with children involved and active bond conditions.

Here’s what’s likely happening and what you can do right now:

First, on the no-contact order  
If your husband has a no-contact condition as part of his bond, that usually means he legally cannot communicate with you directly. So using a third party like his father is actually smart and protective on your end. Keep doing that, and keep everything documented. You’re handling that part correctly.

Second, why things may feel “stuck”  
When discovery is past due, one of two things is usually happening:  
Either his attorney has not produced what’s required yet, or your attorney has not taken action to enforce it.  

There are formal steps your attorney *should* be taking right now, like:  
- Filing a Motion to Compel (forcing the other side to turn over discovery)  
- Requesting a hearing date  
- Pushing the court to enforce deadlines  

If none of that is happening, that’s where the breakdown is. Not hearing anything at all is a red flag.

Third, your attorney not responding  
You should not feel bad following up every two weeks. In a case like this, especially with kids and safety concerns, you deserve consistent updates.

At this point, I would shift from “checking in” to something more direct and time-bound. Send something like this:

“I need an update on the status of discovery, next steps, and what actions are being taken to move my case forward. If I do not hear back by [specific date within 48 hours], I will need to consider alternative representation to ensure my case is being actively handled.”

That’s not aggressive, it’s appropriate.

Fourth, what you can do immediately  
- Call the office, not just email. Ask to speak to a paralegal or office manager if your attorney is unavailable  
- Request a copy of your case file and any filings to date  
- Ask specifically: “Has a Motion to Compel been filed?”  
- If not, ask why  

Fifth, if you continue to get no response  
You may need to consult another family law attorney and potentially switch counsel. Many will do a quick consult and can tell you very quickly if your case is being properly handled or not.

Since you’re in Tennessee, here are a few places to start if you need backup guidance:

- entity["organization","Tennessee Bar Association","state bar organization"] referral service  
- entity["organization","Legal Aid Society of Middle Tennessee and the Cumberlands","nonprofit legal aid"] (especially if cost is a concern)  
- entity["organization","Nashville Bar Association","local bar association"] lawyer referral line  

They can connect you with responsive family law attorneys quickly.

Lastly, trust your instincts  
The fact that you feel lost usually means communication has already broken down too far. A good attorney keeps you informed, especially in a situation involving safety, children, and a no-contact order.

If you want, I can help you draft a stronger message to your attorney or help you prepare what to say on a consult call so you walk in confident and in control.
